result: The authors developed a high-throughput method to simultaneously track family membership, division number, and cell phenotype in HSPCs. Bone marrow cells were isolated, enriched for c-Kit+ cells, stained with antibodies and CellTrace dyes in four distinct combinations, then single cells from three HSPC populations (SLAM-HSC, ST-HSC, MPP) were sorted into wells and cultured for 24 or 48 hours before analysis.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C96-C98, C101 describe a well-documented experimental workflow with appropriate controls and ethical approval. The method is illustrated in Figure 1 and described in detail in the Materials and Methods. The approach is technically sound and builds on established techniques (CellTrace dyes, flow cytometry, index sorting).

result: From 600 seeded cells of each ancestor type, recovery rates were 71% for SLAM-HSCs (358 families, 648 cells), 69% for ST-HSCs (343 families, 592 cells), and 49% for MPPs (246 families, 362 cells). Only 2.8% of recovered families (27 families) were excluded due to cell numbers inconsistent with single-cell origin. Recovery per well was estimated at ~70%.
evaluation: Claims C6-C9, C99 provide quantitative recovery data that demonstrates the technical success of the method. The low exclusion rate (2.8%) validates the single-cell sorting fidelity. The recovery estimates are clearly stated and the data shown in Figure 2A supports these numbers.

result: A diversity of myeloid cell types was observed from all three ancestor types, including GMP, CMP/MEP, PreMegE, and late MPs. SLAM-HSCs and ST-HSCs rarely differentiated into Flt3+ MPPs. Some ST-HSCs and MPPs acquired CD150 expression (not due to antibody carryover). IL-3/IL-6 addition did not affect SLAM-HSC differentiation patterns but significantly altered ST-HSC and MPP differentiation, particularly affecting MPP progeny.
evaluation: Claims C10-C16, C24 describe differentiation outcomes supported by data in Figures 2A, 2D and appropriate controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Statistical testing via permutation tests is appropriate. The functional validation of cell types in methylcellulose culture (Figure 2B,C) strengthens phenotypic assignments. The observation that IL-3/IL-6 differentially affects cell types is consistent with prior literature (C16 cites Lui et al., 2014).

result: Substantial heterogeneity in division was observed between families (0-6 divisions). At 24h most cells were undivided or had divided once; by 48h over 90% had divided at least once. IL-3/IL-6 significantly increased proliferation for all three ancestor types. A substantial fraction of undivided ancestors differentiated (36.5% SLAM-HSCs, 61.1% ST-HSCs, 35.6% MPPs without IL-3/IL-6), with SLAM-HSCs preferentially differentiating to PreMegE. High Sca-1 expression correlated with reduced differentiation in undivided SLAM-HSCs.
evaluation: Claims C17-C23 are supported by data in Figures 2A, 2E, 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3. The observations are consistent with previous reports (C18 cites Roch et al., 2017; C21 cites Roch et al., 2015 and Grinenko et al., 2018; C22 cites Grinenko et al., 2018; C23 cites Schulte et al., 2015). Statistical analyses using permutation tests are appropriate for the data structure.

result: After first division, 70.7% of cells had symmetric fates. MPPs showed mostly symmetric undifferentiated fates (51.4%), ST-HSCs mostly symmetric differentiated fates (59.5%), and SLAM-HSCs showed both symmetric (32.1%) and asymmetric (10.7%) undifferentiated fates. Asymmetric fates occurred in 28.6% of SLAM-HSCs, 28.6% of ST-HSCs, and 31.4% of MPPs. No statistical difference was found between culture conditions (±IL-3/IL-6) for symmetric vs asymmetric fate patterns.
evaluation: Claims C25-C30 quantify first division outcomes from experimental data shown in Figure 2G. The proportions are clearly calculated and the observation of ~30% asymmetric division is consistent with previous reports (C29 cites Suda et al., 1984). The statistical analysis (C30) is appropriate. However, the authors acknowledge that asymmetric fate cannot be distinguished from symmetric fate followed by differentiation without division of one daughter cell, which is an important caveat.

result: Families showed high concordance in division progression: 81% of families that divided more than once had all cells in the same generation (range=0), and only 1.8% had cells more than one generation apart. Mathematical modeling accounting for sampling effects estimated correlation coefficients of 70-90% for division decisions within families (except MPPs without IL-3/IL-6). Division progression is highly concordant within families but heterogeneous between families.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by data in Figure 2H and mathematical modeling described in Materials and Methods. The beta-binomial model appropriately accounts for sampling effects (recovery rate ~70%). The high correlation coefficients (70-90%) quantitatively demonstrate within-family concordance. The modeling approach is mathematically sound and the best-fit parameters are shown to recapitulate the observed range distributions.

result: Differentiation generally progressed with division. UMAP visualization revealed smooth transitions from SLAM-HSCs to differentiated cells, with GMPs/MPs on the top left and CMP/MEP/PreMegE on the top right. More differentiated cells appeared at 48h than 24h, suggesting 24-48h is required for full differentiation to Sca1- progenitors. All three ancestor types remained present at 48h. SLAM-HSCs were primed toward CMP/MEP/PreMegE production, MPPs toward GMPs, and ST-HSCs showed even distribution. PreMegEs were generated from SLAM-HSCs without division or in 1-3 divisions.
evaluation: Claims C35-C43 describe UMAP analysis of differentiation trajectories shown in Figures 3A-D. The UMAP method is appropriate for visualizing high-dimensional flow cytometry data. The observation that differentiation progresses with division is consistent with prior work (C35 cites Upadhaya et al., 2018). The smooth transitions and lineage priming patterns are clearly visible in the figures. The computational methods are adequately described (C100).

result: At 24h most families contained only one cell type, but at 48h more families produced multiple cell types, indicating downstream asymmetries occur after largely symmetric first divisions. Permutation tests showed families exhibited significantly more similarity in cell types than expected by chance at both timepoints. Within-family similarity is visible as co-localization on UMAP. HSPC families are highly concordant in division and share similar differentiation outcomes, while population-level diversity arises from heterogeneity across families.
evaluation: Claims C44-C48 are supported by data in Figures 4A-C. The permutation test framework is appropriate for testing family effects while accounting for familial dependencies. The statistical significance is clearly demonstrated. The UMAP visualization (Figure 4C) provides visual confirmation of within-family similarity. The conclusion (C48) appropriately synthesizes the findings.

result: Ancestral surface marker expression correlated with offspring marker expression, supporting that ancestral markers are instructive for within-family homogeneity. For SLAM-HSCs, CD48 correlated positively with division (strongest at 24h), Sca-1 negatively, and c-Kit positively at 48h. For ST-HSCs and MPPs, phenotypic markers showed no strong correlation with division progression, indicating need for other markers.
evaluation: Claims C49-C55 are supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B and statistical testing in Figure 4D. The Jonckheere trend test is appropriate for testing ordered relationships. The finding that ancestral expression predicts offspring behavior is important, but the authors appropriately note limitations (C55, C77) - markers don't fully explain ST-HSC/MPP division concordance. Spearman correlations are reported with confidence intervals.

result: For SLAM-HSCs, Sca-1 expression positively correlated with self-renewal and negatively with PreMegE production at both timepoints and conditions. c-Kit showed inverse dependency to Sca-1 at 48h. CD48 correlated negatively with self-renewal and positively with PreMegE production when IL-3/IL-6 were added. High Sca-1 and low c-Kit expression lead to less division and differentiation, potentially resulting in better engraftment. CD48's relationship to differentiation is dependent on extrinsic signals.
evaluation: Claims C56-C60 describe correlations between ancestral marker expression and differentiation outcomes for SLAM-HSCs, supported by data in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The conclusions are consistent with multiple prior studies (C59 cites Wilson et al., 2015; Grinenko et al., 2014; Morcos et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2014). The observation that CD48's effect depends on cytokines (C60) is novel and appropriately contrasts with prior literature (cites Pietras et al., 2015; Akinduro et al., 2018).

result: For ST-HSCs, ancestral CD48 and Sca-1 levels correlated negatively and positively, respectively, with de-differentiation to SLAM-HSC in IL-3/IL-6 conditions at both timepoints. Differentiation to GMP (occurring only at 48h) correlated positively with CD48 and negatively with Sca-1. GMP differentiation depends on parental CD48/Sca-1 levels, while de-differentiation to SLAM-HSC depends on both extrinsic factors (IL-3/IL-6) and intrinsic ancestral CD48/Sca-1 levels.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by statistical analysis shown in Figures 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The observation that GMP differentiation correlates with CD48/Sca-1 is consistent with prior work (C62 cites Morcos et al., 2017). The distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic dependencies (C63) is an important inference appropriately drawn from the differential effects of IL-3/IL-6 on different differentiation outcomes.

result: MPP to GMP differentiation (observed by 48h) correlated negatively with ancestral Sca-1 in both cocktails and with Flt3 only without IL-3/IL-6. With IL-3/IL-6, MPP to GMP differentiation positively correlated with c-Kit. MPP to CMP/MEP differentiation occurred only at 48h without IL-3/IL-6 and correlated positively with c-Kit. GMP differentiation from MPP depends on intrinsic Sca-1 levels, while CMP/MEP differentiation depends on both extrinsic factors (IL-3/IL-6) and intrinsic c-Kit levels.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68 are supported by statistical analysis in Figure 4E. The negative correlation with Sca-1 is consistent with prior work (C64 cites Morcos et al., 2017). The differential dependencies on intrinsic vs extrinsic factors (C68) represent an important mechanistic insight appropriately inferred from the condition-specific correlations observed.

result: Concordance in division and similarity in fate within families is partially explained by ancestral surface marker expression, but both intrinsic and extrinsic factors direct familial fate. Despite population-level heterogeneity, offspring from single ancestors are highly concordant in division and exhibit familial effects on differentiation. Restriction in cell types within families is propagated primarily through symmetric first divisions. The overall collection of cell types is composed of homogeneous families from heterogeneous ancestors.
evaluation: Claims C69-C72 synthesize the major findings of the study. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective evidence from division concordance (C31-C34), differentiation similarity (C44-C48), and marker correlations (C49-C68). The conclusion that diversity arises from heterogeneous families rather than within-family diversification (C72) is a key conceptual advance supported by the data.

result: Current assumptions in the field are that cell type diversity results from diversification within every family and that cells behave independently (as assumed by trajectory inference methods). The findings establish that unmeasured familial dependencies exist and call for revision of the independence assumption. Ancestral surface markers partially predict familial properties, but markers explaining ST-HSC/MPP division progression are not contained within the phenotyping panel. Extrinsic factors like cytokines can alter familial effects.
evaluation: Claims C73-C78 place the findings in context of current field assumptions and identify limitations. The characterization of current assumptions (C73-C74) is accurate and appropriately cited (Trapnell et al., 2014; Bendall et al., 2014). The call for revision (C75) is justified by the strong evidence for familial dependencies and is consistent with prior lineage priming observations (cites Müller-Sieburg et al., 2002; Perié and Duffy, 2016; Paul et al., 2016; Hoppe et al., 2016). The acknowledgment of limitations (C77) is appropriate.

result: The broad range of HSPC engraftment and proliferation capacities in transplantation could be consequences of heterogeneity in engrafted families. Altered culture conditions might reduce or enhance between-family heterogeneity and possibly improve transplantation outcomes if leading to more self-renewal divisions. Changing the composition of committed HSPC populations might alter lineage production balance with therapeutic applications for leukemia and genetic immune disorders.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are speculative suggestions for future applications. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the findings, they are explicitly speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION) and have not been tested. The suggestions are plausible but would require substantial additional experimental validation including in vivo transplantation studies to be considered supported.

result: Prior work has established that HSCs can sequentially reconstitute blood in multiple hosts, must self-renew through symmetric and asymmetric division influenced by extrinsic signals, and that MPPs can self-renew. HSCs can differentiate without division. Recent studies show HSCs are heterogeneous in lineage output, with most being lineage-restricted or biased. Some HSCs produce only megakaryocytes or only myeloid/megakaryocyte/erythroid cells. MPPs also show heterogeneous restricted lineage patterns, suggesting early lineage restriction in the HSC/MPP pool.
evaluation: Claims C82-C95 summarize prior literature to provide context for the current study. All claims are appropriately cited with specific references. This represents accurate characterization of the field's current understanding based on published work. These are background claims rather than new findings from this study.

result: UMAP was performed on arcsinh(x/100) transformed fluorescence intensity values using the R UMAP package (version 0.2.0.0) with default parameters.
evaluation: Claim C100 describes the computational method for UMAP analysis. The transformation and parameters are clearly specified, allowing reproducibility. The arcsinh transformation is appropriate for flow cytometry data. However, the use of default parameters without justification or exploration of parameter sensitivity is a minor limitation. The version number is specified which aids reproducibility.
